A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CGRO research by the same authors. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial restructuring.

before.justification: v1 reports original MNIST and CIFAR10 experiments on loss landscapes, training dynamics and flatness in Section 6 and Figures 2–3.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments in Appendices A–B and adds original model-capacity experiments and synthetic-data simulations in Section 6.

M1.justification: The analyzed framework changes from a cubic CNN with m = polylog(d) and surrogate-based GTA to a tied ReLU^q CNN with m = Θ(N) and maximization of the current model's loss over signal-aligned perturbations. Although the cubic special case remains closely related, the model family, capacity and specified training procedure are substantively revised.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual simulation on synthetic patch-structured binary-classification data, which appeared only as a theoretical setting in v1. MNIST and CIFAR10 remain covered, including the original experiments retained in Appendix A.

E2.justification: v2 Section 6.1 adds a qualitative comparison with standard training: small MNIST networks reportedly learn an accurate clean classifier under standard training but collapse to constant predictions under adversarial training. This comparison is reported in prose; Tables 1–2 do not introduce a numerical benchmark against competing defenses.

E3.justification: The new capacity study uses scaled LeNet-5 and WideResNet-34 models, PGD training, 100/200 epochs and MNIST perturbation radius 0.3. The synthetic study introduces N = 20, d = 100, 100 training iterations and PGD evaluation. These are additional protocols; the earlier 20/15-epoch landscape experiments remain in Appendix A.

E4.justification: v2 adds model-capacity sensitivity experiments examining collapse, memorization and generalization. It also directly tracks signal learning and minimum, maximum and average noise memorization to examine the proposed training phases. The earlier perturbation-radius and flatness analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty bars. The new minimum/maximum/average curves summarize noise memorization across training examples, not uncertainty across runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds Tables 1–2 and Figure 2. New CIFAR10 robust test accuracies range from 43.39% to 50.08% across the reported model sizes. The synthetic experiment reports 100% clean and robust training accuracy, 98.5% clean test accuracy and 17.5% robust test accuracy. These are new results, not improvements over matched v1 settings; the original landscape curves are retained.

T1.justification: v2 replaces fixed signal/noise exponents with broader ranges in Assumption 5.7 and states q-dependent dynamics bounds. It changes robust training error from error on generated adversarial samples to a worst-case perturbation-ball definition and relaxes the clean-classifier assumption from zero error to o(1). These revise theoretical scope; the detailed dynamics proof still specializes to q = 3, and the flatness bound is retained.

C1.justification: The central partial-feature-learning/noise-memorization explanation and polynomial-versus-exponential complexity claim remain. v2 states the dynamics contribution for a broader learner and parameter regime and centers its headline contributions on complexity and three-stage dynamics. The global-flatness bound remains in Appendix B but is omitted from the abstract and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 newly discusses failure of clean generalization at low signal-to-noise ratios, explains the restriction to one meaningful patch and discusses possible extensions. It also interprets the newly observed collapse of small adversarially trained models. The central explanation through partial feature learning and robust memorization remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 provides filter and hidden-layer sizes, widening factors, training budgets, NVIDIA RTX 4090 hardware and explicit synthetic-data and optimization parameters. This substantially expands experimental documentation. Conversely, Appendix A drops the earlier architectural specificity of LeNet5 and Resnet9, calling them LeNet and Resnet.

R1.justification: v2 adds supporting references including Chidambaram et al. (2023), Kou et al. (2023), Cao et al. (2021), Frei et al. (2022) and Wide Residual Networks. It removes references associated with the GTA and transferability discussion. The principal positioning relative to feature-learning theory and robust representation complexity remains.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution list and conclusion are rewritten. v2 adds an expanded preliminaries section, places representation complexity before training dynamics, reorganizes the dynamics exposition into phases and moves the original experimental and flatness sections into appendices. This substantially changes the narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text and references from one column to two columns, adds a three-panel Figure 2 and two result tables, and relocates the original Figures 2–3 as appendix Figures 3–4. Figures, equations and surrounding text are extensively rearranged.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful capacity tests, direct feature-learning measurements and clearer organization. However, its definition of robust training error over the full perturbation ball is paired with a proof based on restricted attacks. Section 6.2 also claims conformity with Assumption 5.7 while setting δ = α = 10, although that assumption requires δ < α. These unresolved mismatches weaken the claimed validation, preventing a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.
